passage:
In 2015, a group of researchers tried something unusual. Instead of running new experiments, they repeated one hundred well-known psychology studies to see whether the same results would appear again. Only about thirty-six percent produced findings clearly similar to the originals. The report shocked many scientists and started what journalists soon called the replication crisis.

Some researchers argue that the crisis has been exaggerated. A failed repetition, they say, does not prove the first study wrong, since small differences in place, season, or participants can change an outcome. Others take a harder view. Professor Dana Klein notes that universities reward scientists for surprising discoveries rather than for careful checking, and that journals rarely publish results showing that nothing happened. Under such pressure, weak findings are almost certain to spread.

Changes are now under way. More than three thousand journals ask researchers to register their plans before collecting data, so methods cannot be adjusted afterwards to make results look better. Some funding bodies also set aside money purely for repetition studies. Progress remains slow, yet most scientists agree that a field willing to test itself in public is healthier than one that never looks back.
stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage as a whole?
options: Psychology experiments are no longer accepted by serious academic journals anywhere.
Scientists have proved that surprising discoveries are almost always completely false.
A large repetition project revealed weaknesses in research practice and led to reforms.
Universities have stopped rewarding researchers who publish any new findings at all.
explain_zh: 全文先談 2015 年的重複實驗計畫、再談爭論，最後談改革措施，主軸就是「重複研究揭露了問題並帶來改變」。選項 A、D 文中沒說；B 過度推論，文中只說重複成功率低，沒說驚人發現一定是假的。主旨題要找能涵蓋全部段落的敘述。

When Ireland introduced a small charge on plastic shopping bags in 2002, few officials expected much. Within a year, the number of bags handed out at checkouts had fallen by more than ninety percent, and the money collected was directed into an environmental fund. Governments elsewhere noticed, and today over eighty countries limit single-use bags in some way.

Yet environmental groups warn that such measures can create a comfortable illusion. Shopping bags make up only a tiny share of plastic waste; packaging, bottles and fishing equipment account for far more. A Norwegian study found that shoppers who paid for bags often bought more bottled drinks on the same trip, apparently feeling that they had already done their part for the planet. Researchers call this pattern moral licensing.

Supporters of the charge reply that its real value is educational. Every visit to a supermarket reminds people that waste has a price, and that habit spreads to other choices. They also point to deposit-return schemes for bottles, which recover more than ninety percent of containers in Norway and Germany. The lesson, they argue, is not that small policies fail, but that they must form part of a wider plan rather than a substitute for one.
stem: Which statement best expresses the central argument that the passage as a whole develops?
options: Ireland's charge on plastic bags failed to reduce the number of bags used in shops.
Plastic bottles are far more damaging to ocean life than any other form of waste.
Charges on bags work, but they should be judged as one part of a larger effort.
Environmental groups now oppose every kind of government action on plastic waste.
explain_zh: 文章先講袋子收費成功，再講它的侷限與道德許可效應，最後說小政策必須是整體計畫的一部分，所以 C 最完整。A 與第一段數據相反；B 文中沒有比較海洋危害；D 過度延伸，環保團體只是提醒別自滿。主旨題選能同時容納正反兩面的敘述。

passage:
In 2016 a school district in Seattle moved the start of its high-school classes from 7:50 to 8:45 in the morning. Researchers from the University of Washington then asked students to wear light sensors and activity monitors for two weeks. On average the teenagers slept thirty-four minutes longer each night, and their grades in the classes studied rose by about four percent. Attendance improved as well, especially among students from poorer families.

Sleep scientists were not surprised. During adolescence the body clock shifts later, so asking a fifteen-year-old to concentrate at eight in the morning is, as one researcher puts it, rather like asking an adult to work at five.

Not everyone welcomes the change, however. Head teachers point out that later classes push sports practice and part-time jobs into the evening, and that parents who leave for work at seven must find somewhere for their children to wait. Bus companies serving several schools would need extra vehicles. Supporters answer that these are problems of timetabling rather than of principle, and that few other reforms deliver such clear gains for so little money.
stem: Which of the following best summarises what the whole passage is mainly about?
options: A later start to the school day brought measurable benefits but raised practical difficulties.
Teenagers living in Seattle sleep considerably less than teenagers in any other city.
Sports practice and part-time jobs should be removed from the school timetable entirely.
Sleep scientists strongly disagree with each other about when the body clock changes.
explain_zh: 前兩段講延後上課的好處與科學依據，第三段講校長與客運公司的現實困難，所以主旨是「有效果但有實務問題」。B 文中沒有跨城市比較；C 是誤讀反對意見；D 與「睡眠科學家並不意外」矛盾。主旨題要同時涵蓋正反兩面。

Cameras that recognise faces are no longer science fiction. In 2019 police in South Wales tested a system that compared passers-by with a list of wanted people. Supporters said it would catch criminals quickly; critics said it turned an ordinary street into a checkpoint. A court later ruled that the trial had gone too far, and the force was told to write clearer rules.

The technology itself has improved sharply. Error rates in laboratory tests fell by about ninety-five percent between 2014 and 2020. Yet accuracy in a quiet laboratory is not the same as accuracy in a crowded railway station, where light, angle and movement all matter. Independent tests in the United States also found that systems identified darker-skinned women wrongly far more often than lighter-skinned men, because the photographs used to train them were not balanced.

Some governments have responded with complete bans in public spaces; others require a judge's permission before a camera may be used at all. Technology companies are themselves divided, and two large firms have paused sales to police departments. What almost everyone accepts is that the rules cannot be left to the engineers who build these systems.
stem: Which of the following best states the main idea that the passage as a whole presents?
options: Face recognition has advanced quickly, but its public use raises problems that remain unsolved.
Police forces in Britain have now abandoned every form of camera technology in public.
Laboratory testing is the only reliable method of measuring how well a technology works.
Technology companies fully agree that these systems should be sold to anyone who asks.
explain_zh: 全文一面說技術進步很快（錯誤率大降），一面說法院判決、偏誤與規範爭議都還沒解決，所以 A 最貼切。B 與文中只暫停販售、要求訂規則不同；C 第二段正好說實驗室不等於真實環境；D 與 companies are divided 矛盾。

passage:
Antibiotics changed medicine. Before the 1940s a scratch from a garden thorn could kill a healthy adult; afterwards, infections that had once emptied hospital wards could be cured in days. The victory, however, was never permanent. Bacteria reproduce so quickly that a colony may pass through several generations in a single afternoon, and any individual that survives a drug passes its advantage on.

The scale of the problem is now hard to ignore. A review commissioned by the British government estimated that drug-resistant infections were linked to about 1.27 million deaths worldwide in 2019, and warned that the figure could climb steeply by 2050. Farming plays a part too: in some countries more than half of all antibiotics produced are given to healthy animals to make them grow faster.

What is missing is not scientific knowledge but money. Developing a new antibiotic costs well over a billion dollars, and the moment one appears doctors are told to keep it in reserve, which is exactly the opposite of what a company needs in order to earn its investment back. Several governments are therefore testing subscription payments, in which a health service pays a fixed annual fee for access to a drug whether or not it is used.

passage:
Who owns the past? In 1897 British soldiers removed thousands of brass and ivory works from the Kingdom of Benin, in what is now southern Nigeria. The objects were sold across Europe and America, and for more than a century most museums treated the question of ownership as closed.

That confidence has weakened. Since 2021 institutions in Germany, Scotland and the United States have transferred hundreds of Benin works back to Nigeria, and a museum in Lagos is being built to house them. Supporters of return argue that an object made for a royal court in West Africa cannot be fully understood inside a glass case two thousand kilometres away, and that keeping it simply continues the original theft.

Opponents rarely defend the raid itself. They argue instead that large museums let visitors compare many civilisations in one building, that objects are safer in rooms where temperature is controlled, and that a single return may lead to thousands of further claims. Some curators suggest long-term loans as a compromise. Critics reply that a loan still leaves the borrower's side deciding when the object may go home, which is precisely the point at issue.

Visitors to large museums clearly prefer African art to art made in other regions.

passage:
Between June and December 2022, sixty-one British companies moved their staff to a four-day week with no cut in pay. The trial, organised with researchers from Cambridge and Boston College, covered about 2,900 employees in banks, restaurants and small factories. When it ended, fifty-six firms decided to carry on, and revenue across the group was roughly the same as in the previous year. Reported levels of burnout fell sharply, and the number of staff resigning dropped by more than half.

Economists urge caution. Companies that volunteer for such a trial are hardly typical: they tend to be small, profitable and already interested in flexible working. Measuring output is also difficult in offices, where a shorter week may simply push work into the remaining four days rather than remove it.

Even so, the direction of travel seems clear. Working hours in rich countries have fallen steadily for a hundred and fifty years, usually after similar warnings of ruin. The interesting question may no longer be whether the week will shorten, but which industries can manage it first, and what becomes of those that cannot.

In a small California food shop in 1995, two psychologists set up a tasting table. On some days they offered twenty-four kinds of jam; on other days, only six. The larger display attracted more passers-by, but of those who stopped, only three percent went on to buy a jar. At the smaller display nearly thirty percent did. The study became one of the most quoted pieces of research in modern psychology, and the phrase choice overload entered everyday speech.

Later work has been less tidy. When researchers combined fifty similar experiments, the average effect was close to zero. The size of a choice seems to matter only under particular conditions: when the shopper has no clear preference, when the products are hard to compare, and when a wrong decision feels expensive.

For businesses the practical lesson is not to offer less but to organise better. Online shops selling thousands of products keep their customers by sorting them into clear categories and suggesting a sensible starting point. The real difficulty, researchers now believe, was never the number of options; it was the effort of holding them all in mind at the same time.

Barcelona's superblocks began as lines of paint. In 2016 the city grouped nine blocks of its grid together, allowed only residents' vehicles into the inner streets, and gave the reclaimed space to benches, trees and children. Traffic inside the first superblock fell by more than half. Monitors recorded a drop of about a quarter in nitrogen dioxide, a gas produced mainly by diesel engines and linked to asthma.

The response was not universally warm. Shopkeepers feared that customers who could not park would go elsewhere, and delivery drivers complained about longer routes. Surveys taken two years later found that most local businesses reported steady or rising sales, but the early anger was real and it slowed the programme.

Planners elsewhere have watched closely. Critics warn that a design suited to Barcelona's regular nineteenth-century grid may not transfer to cities with winding medieval lanes or wide American avenues. Others point to a deeper worry: when a street becomes pleasant, rents rise, and the very families a scheme was meant to serve may be pushed out. Barcelona now reserves part of the new housing in these districts at controlled rents.

For four hundred years Britain had no wild beavers. Hunted for their fur and for a substance used in medicine, they vanished in the sixteenth century, and the wetlands they had built slowly drained away. In 2015 a small population was found living on the River Otter in Devon, and the government allowed the animals to stay while scientists watched what they did.

The results have been striking. Beaver dams hold water back in dry weather and slow it during storms; in one monitored village, peak flows after heavy rain fell by around thirty percent. The pools behind the dams trapped soil and fertiliser washing off nearby farmland, and the number of water plants and insects rose sharply. Frogs returned in numbers that nobody had expected.

Farmers are less enthusiastic. A dam in the wrong place can flood a field of vegetables or block a drainage ditch, and compensation schemes have been slow to pay. Ecologists accept that the animals cannot simply be released and then forgotten. Wherever beavers spread, someone has to be paid to manage them, and that cost is rarely counted when a project is first announced.

Sunlight and wind are now the cheapest sources of new electricity in most of the world. The awkward part is that neither arrives on demand. On a still winter evening a country with a large wind fleet may produce almost nothing, while on a bright spring afternoon it may generate more than its grid can absorb, and operators are paid to switch turbines off.

Storage is the obvious answer, and lithium batteries have fallen in price by roughly ninety percent since 2010. Yet batteries are built for hours, not for weeks. Engineers therefore separate two problems: the daily shift of solar power from noon to evening, which batteries handle well, and the seasonal gap between a cloudy December and a sunny June, which they cannot.

Answers to the second problem range from pumped hydropower, an old technology limited by geography, to hydrogen made from surplus electricity and burned months later. Hydrogen loses more than half of the energy put into it, a figure critics find damning. Supporters reply that wasting cheap surplus power matters far less than having no power at all on the coldest night of the year.

When a high-speed line opened between Madrid and Barcelona in 2008, the journey fell from about six hours to two and a half. Within five years the train carried more than sixty percent of travellers on the route, a share that airlines had held almost entirely before. France later banned domestic flights wherever a train could cover the same trip in under two and a half hours, and other governments are studying the idea.

The environmental case looks simple. A passenger on a high-speed train is responsible for roughly a twentieth of the carbon dioxide produced by the same journey in an aircraft. Yet building a line is itself expensive in carbon: tunnels, bridges and concrete can take a decade of operation to pay back. Lines that carry few passengers may never do so.

Distance matters as well. Beyond about four hours of rail travel most passengers return to aircraft, which is why the largest gains appear on medium routes rather than very long ones. Between 2005 and 2022 the United States lost more than a quarter of its newspapers, most of them small weeklies serving towns of a few thousand people. Researchers at Northwestern University describe the result as a news desert: a community with no reliable source of information about its own schools, courts and budgets.

The effects are measurable and slightly surprising. After a local paper closes, fewer candidates stand for municipal office and fewer residents vote in local elections. In 1950 the average woman on Earth had about five children; today the figure is close to 2.2, and in South Korea it has fallen below one. Falling fertility is usually explained by education, urban housing costs and the wider availability of contraception. What is less often noticed is how fast the change has been. France took roughly a hundred and fifty years to move from six children to two; Iran did it in about twenty.

Speed matters because a society adjusts slowly. Schools built for one generation stand half empty for the next, and a pension system designed when four workers supported each retired person behaves very differently when the figure is two.

Governments have tried to reverse the trend with cash payments, longer parental leave and free childcare. The evidence suggests that such policies shift the timing of births more than the final number, though the Nordic countries show that good childcare and secure work can at least prevent fertility from sliding further. Demographers increasingly argue that the sensible aim is not a higher birth rate but a society organised for the population it will actually have.

Low Earth orbit is becoming crowded. In 2010 about a thousand working satellites circled the planet; the number is now well above nine thousand, and several companies plan constellations of tens of thousands more. Alongside them travel an estimated thirty-six thousand pieces of debris larger than ten centimetres, and millions of fragments too small to track.

At orbital speed a fragment the size of a coin carries the energy of a small car crash. In 2009 a dead Russian satellite struck an American communications satellite, producing more than two thousand new pieces in a single afternoon. Researchers describe a possible chain reaction, first suggested by Donald Kessler in 1978, in which each collision creates the debris that causes the next one.

Cleaning up is technically possible. A European mission plans to capture an old rocket part using four mechanical arms, and other teams are testing nets and harpoons. None of these methods is cheap, and each raises an awkward question: a device able to remove an enemy's satellite is hard to distinguish from a weapon. The law has not kept pace, and objects in orbit still belong to whoever launched them.
stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea that runs through the entire passage?
options: Orbits around the Earth are filling with debris, and the remedies raise new difficulties.
Collisions between satellites have already made all space travel completely impossible.
European engineers have now solved the problem of removing old rocket parts safely.
The number of working satellites in orbit has fallen sharply since the year 2010.
explain_zh: 文章依序說明軌道擁擠、碰撞連鎖反應、清除技術與隨之而來的軍事與法律問題，所以選 A。B 太極端；C 與 plans to capture 這個未完成式不符；D 與「從一千顆增加到九千顆以上」相反。

Israel now takes more than half of its drinking water from the sea. Desalination plants along the coast push seawater through membranes at high pressure, and the cost of the process has fallen from about a dollar per cubic metre in 1990 to roughly fifty cents today. For a country with a dry climate and a growing population, the technology has removed a source of constant anxiety.

The method is not free of difficulty. Removing salt is energy-hungry, and where the electricity comes from gas or coal the water arrives with a substantial carbon cost. Each litre of fresh water also leaves behind a litre of brine, twice as salty as the sea, which is usually returned offshore. Studies near plants in the Gulf report lower oxygen levels and fewer bottom-living species wherever the currents are weak.

Engineers point out that these problems are local and manageable, while a shortage of water is neither. Critics answer that the real danger is complacency: a city able to manufacture water may see little reason to repair leaking pipes or to price water sensibly. In Australia, several plants built during a long drought stood idle for years once the rain returned.
stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea that the whole passage sets out?
options: Desalination is far too expensive for any country except Israel to consider using.
Shortages of drinking water have now disappeared from the countries around the Gulf.
Desalination solves a serious problem but brings costs that have to be managed.
Leaking pipes are the main cause of water shortages in countries with dry climates.
explain_zh: 第一段講成本下降與解決缺水焦慮，第二段講能源與鹵水的代價，第三段講工程師與批評者的爭論，合起來就是 C。A 與成本減半的趨勢相反；B 文中只提到海灣地區的海洋影響；D 只是批評者舉的例子之一。

In 2016 a small portrait long labelled workshop of Rembrandt was re-examined with a scanner that reads the chemistry of paint layer by layer. Beneath the visible surface lay a first sketch full of corrections, the kind an artist makes while inventing a composition rather than copying one. The picture was reattributed, and its insurance value rose by a factor of forty.

Such reversals are common. Roughly one painting in five in older European collections has changed its attribution at least once, and the direction is not always upward. Science has narrowed the arguments without ending them: chemistry can date a pigment and reveal a hidden drawing, yet it cannot say which hand held the brush in a workshop where assistants were trained to imitate the master.

Some curators find the whole exercise misplaced. A painting that moved visitors on Monday, they argue, is no worse on Friday because a name has changed. Others reply that this is sentimental. Money follows attribution, and so does scholarship: a work carrying a famous name is studied, lent and restored, while an anonymous panel of equal quality may stay in a store room for decades.

options: Modern scanners have made every disagreement about attribution impossible to sustain.

Museums ought to stop lending paintings by famous artists to other galleries.

For half a century athletes were told to stretch before exercise. The advice seemed obvious: a warm, loose muscle ought to be harder to tear. When researchers finally tested it, the result was awkward. A review of more than a hundred studies found that static stretching before activity had no measurable effect on injury rates, and that holding a stretch for over a minute slightly reduced the power a muscle could produce immediately afterwards.

One large study of footballers found that a twenty-minute strength programme performed twice a week cut hamstring injuries by roughly half.

Old advice dies slowly. Stretching feels pleasant, it costs nothing, and a coach who abandons a familiar ritual has to explain why. Sports scientists are careful to add that stretching does no harm and remains valuable for gymnasts and dancers, who need a range of movement that other athletes do not. The mistake was never the exercise itself; it was the promise attached to it.

Children are said to pick up languages effortlessly, and adults to struggle. The picture is more complicated than that. In a study of two-thirds of a million English learners, researchers found that the ability to reach native-like grammar does decline with age, but that the fall begins later than expected, at around seventeen, and is gradual rather than sudden.

Adults also enjoy advantages that are easy to overlook. They already understand how language works, they can use a dictionary, and they can study deliberately for an hour instead of waiting for exposure. During the first year of instruction adults usually progress faster than children; it is over ten years that the child overtakes them.

What matters most, the evidence suggests, is neither age nor talent but the amount of meaningful contact with the language. A learner who reads, listens and speaks for an hour every day will pass one who attends a class twice a week, whatever their ages. This is why immersion programmes work, and also why they sometimes fail: a student may sit in a foreign classroom for a year and, by avoiding conversation, receive very little of the exposure the programme was designed to provide.

Volunteering looks like a simple good. Yet its economics are stranger than they appear. A charity that accepts an untrained volunteer for a single day may spend more on supervision than the work is worth, which is why many organisations now prefer regular helpers to one-off groups. A study of British charities estimated that a volunteer becomes profitable to the organisation only after about forty hours.

Motives matter as well. Surveys consistently find that people who volunteer in order to help others stay far longer than those who volunteer to improve a university application. The second group arrives in large numbers each spring and disappears in June, leaving the charity to recruit all over again.

None of this is an argument against volunteering. In the United Kingdom unpaid work is valued at more than twenty billion pounds a year, and much of it, especially in hospices and in mountain rescue, could not be bought at any price. The argument is rather that goodwill is a resource like any other: it can be wasted by poor planning, and it works best when a volunteer is given something genuinely worth doing.

Japan passed a mark in 2023 that no country had reached before: one person in ten is now eighty or older. The figure is usually reported as a warning, and the strain on pensions and hospitals is real. Less often reported is how much of the assumed crisis rests on a measurement that is quietly out of date.

Policy has begun to catch up. Japan has raised the age at which a pension may be drawn, and about a quarter of Japanese aged between sixty-five and sixty-nine are still in paid work, the highest share among wealthy nations. Critics of these changes note that a factory worker's body wears out sooner than an accountant's, and that raising the age uniformly asks most of those who can give least.
stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea that the passage as a whole puts forward?
options: Japan's pension system is certain to collapse at some point in the next ten years.
People aged over sixty-five should no longer be permitted to take paid employment.

Health in later life has improved by exactly the same amount in every occupation.

Economists once explained the gap between men's and women's pay by pointing to education and hours worked. As women overtook men in university enrolment across most rich countries, that explanation weakened. Recent work points somewhere more specific. Studying Danish records that cover several decades, Kleven and colleagues found that men's and women's earnings move together until the birth of a first child, after which women's income falls by about twenty percent and never fully recovers. Men's earnings barely change at all.

The size of this child penalty varies a great deal. It is smaller where fathers take long periods of leave that cannot be transferred, and larger where school hours are short and childcare is expensive. Culture matters too: the penalty is greater for women whose own mothers stayed at home.

Two conclusions follow. First, policies aimed only at the workplace, such as publishing salary figures, address a small part of what is actually happening. Second, leave that fathers may take but rarely do is unlikely to help; the Danish evidence suggests that only leave reserved for fathers, and lost if it is not used, changes behaviour at home.

options: A large part of the pay gap now appears only after the birth of a first child.
Women in wealthy countries are still far less likely to attend university than men.
Publishing salary figures has already removed the pay gap in several countries.
Danish fathers earn considerably less than fathers in other European countries.
explain_zh: 文章說教育與工時已無法解釋薪資差距，真正的分歧點出現在第一胎出生之後，並依此談政策，所以選 A。B 與 women overtook men in university enrolment 相反；C 與「只針對職場的政策效果有限」矛盾；D 文中沒有跨國比較父親收入。

Before 2020 Venice received about twenty-five million visitors a year, roughly five hundred for every resident. The city has since introduced an entry charge for day trippers on its busiest dates, the first scheme of its kind anywhere. Early figures were not encouraging: arrivals on charged days fell only slightly, and the money collected was smaller than the cost of running the system.

The underlying problem is not the number of visitors but the shape of their spending. A day tripper arrives by coach, buys a sandwich and leaves, while the same street loses the bakeries and repair shops that residents depend on, because a souvenir stall can pay far more rent. Venice has lost more than half of its residents since 1970. Similar patterns can be seen in Barcelona, Kyoto and Dubrovnik.

Some cities have therefore turned from charging tourists to regulating what property may be used for. Barcelona has capped the number of flats licensed for short stays and plans to end them by 2029. Whether such rules survive legal challenge is uncertain, and landlords argue that they merely move the problem to the next district.

Venice has succeeded in reducing the number of day trippers who come to visit it.
Tourists who visit Barcelona spend far more money than tourists who visit Venice.
The resident population of Venice has been growing steadily ever since 1970.
